items.title: The Holistic Survival of Humanity Overrides All
items.abstract: Survival and happiness are the two fundamental core values of humanity, among which survival has absolute priority. The perpetual interests of humanity as a whole completely override individual, partial, and short-term interests of a single generation. From this, a core proposition can be established: the holistic survival of humanity overrides all. This proposition is not a subjective moral advocacy, but an objective law consistent with species survival and civilizational evolution. At present, the global field of existential risk research has long suffered from paradigmatic and normative research gaps. The mainstream academic community relies on probabilistic quantification and risk trade-off frameworks to assess human extinction risk, and has never formed an exclusive research system and value criterion of "absolute priority of survival, zero tolerance, and irreversibility." The probabilistic research paradigm for the risk of technology-induced human extinction, widely adopted in global academia and public decision-making, contains fundamental scientific fallacies. Using the quantitative logic of conventional trial-and-error risk to assess zero-tolerance, irreversible human extinction risk is not only of no research value, but also causes widespread cognitive numbing and indulges the disorderly development of high-risk technologies. Since the advent of industrial civilization, the unchecked growth of disruptive technologies such as artificial intelligence, synthetic biology, nanotechnology, and nuclear technology has completely rewritten humanity's risk landscape, bringing humanity for the first time close to the capability of self-extinction. If the unrestrained development of science and technology continues, humanity will soon be extinct due to technology—at most within two or three hundred years, and at the earliest within this century. This is a scientific conclusion argued on the basis of five axioms and the paradigm of "Extinction Path Analysis + Defense Limit Testing" [14][15]. Any behavior that gambles the holistic survival of humanity in exchange for partial development, technological competition, or commercial dividends is essentially civilizational suicide. Based on this, public policy must thoroughly reconstruct its value system, abandon the probabilistic risk paradigm, and establish a global technology governance system centered on essential risk, zero-tolerance bottom lines, and perpetual survival, so as to fundamentally resolve humanity's ultimate existential crisis.

items.title: The Impact of Ergonomics Training on Work Practices for Ultrasound Technology Students
items.abstract: Ultrasound technologists frequently experience work-related musculoskeletal disorders. This study evaluated the impact of an ergonomics training program on task-related behaviors among ultrasound technology students within an ultrasound education program ( n = 17), and their work practices were evaluated through video analysis. This study identified eight tasks that were usually performed during ultrasound scans and ergonomic training influenced the task sequence and distribution of posture exposure during those tasks. This study also identified several task-related behaviors among participants after training, which included workstation adjustments ( n = 13), taking short breaks during scans ( n = 10), repositioning patients ( n = 6) and task switching to reduce long uninterrupted postures. There was also significantly lower maximum uninterrupted posture duration ( p = .031) and significantly higher task transition frequency ( p = .037) after training. These findings suggest that ergonomic training may positively influence the task behaviors among ultrasound technology students and encourage learning best practice postures while developing technical expertise.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF TECHNOSTRESS AND PSYCHOLOGICAL FACTORS ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF DIGITAL COMPETENCE IN LEGAL EDUCATION
items.abstract: This scientific article provides a comprehensive analysis of the interplay and impact of psychological factors-such as intrinsic motivation, technostress, and «AI anxiety»-on the process of forming and developing digital competence within legal educational institutions. The study examines how «rotational stress» and cognitive overload-arising from the need for future legal professionals to engage regularly and intensively with a multitude of digital platforms (including Moodle, ZiyoNet, Zoom, ChatGPT, and specialized Telegram bots) during their studies-affect both academic performance and psychological well-being. Based on empirical and theoretical analyses, methods for overcoming psychological barriers and cognitive obstacles are substantiated. These methods involve positioning artificial intelligence systems not as rivals or replacements, but as «digital assistants» or «junior partners,» alongside the rational integration of «digital minimalism» principles into educational practice. The findings of this research contribute to the enhancement of digital didactics and pedagogical technologies within legal education.

items.title: The Judge Under Trial: Stress-Testing RART and the Limits of Automated Evaluation at Scale
items.abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) as automated evaluators commonly termed LLM-as-a-Judge introduces a critical question: who evaluates the evaluator? This paper puts the lifecycle framework of Kong et al. [1] on trial, stress-testing its core claims for building, aligning, and monitoring LLM judges in production-scale recommendation explanation systems. We synthesize the core contributions: (1) the identification of a subtle failure mode termed ”right answer, wrong reason,” wherein a judge reaches the correct verdict through unsound reasoning that is invisible to label-agreement dashboards; (2) Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART), a procedure that iteratively refines rubric text using a Meta-Judge to compare judge rationales against human rationales; (3) a fourphase lifecycle-Birth, Training, Deployment, and Monitoring-that anchors LLM judges to human judgment at every stage; and (4) a formal mathematical model stress-tested via Monte Carlo simulation. We provide an open-source implementation of this simulation and analyze its visual output. The simulation confirms RART’s ability to stabilize reasoning alignment but visually reveals methodological vulnerabilities, including a stopping-rule artifact, a severe drift-band calibration problem, and the structural reality of blind-spot leaks. Furthermore, the framework relies on critical unvalidated assumptions-most notably, that the judge and generator do not share blind spots. We conclude that while RART effectively mitigates rubric degradation, it is not a closed-form mathematical solution to Al alignment and ultimately requires continuous human-in-the-loop audits.

items.title: The new constructionism. Papert after Peirce: indexicality, navigational thinking, and learning in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: The arrival of generative AI in every classroom has produced a crisis that is at once technological, epistemological, and pedagogical. We argue that the appropriate response is neither prohibition nor naive adoption, but a principled reconstruction of constructionism for a computational environment that is generative, context-sensitive, and dialogically accessible. Drawing on Peircean semiotics, Papertian constructionism, Polanyi's epistemology, and contemporary neural-network research, we develop a programmatic framework we call the New Constructionism. We make four connected contributions. First, we argue that generative AI introduces an indexical mode of computation: its relation to the empirical world may be direct, mediated, or incomplete, but in a situated human–AI configuration meaning is operationally conditioned by conversational history, artifacts, tools, observations, and action. Second, we introduce a three-dimensional analytical space — semiotic, psycho-epistemological, and pedagogical — in which learning paradigms can be located and compared. Third, we reinterpret the history of programming education as a movement from a predominantly symbolic environment toward a hybrid ecology in which symbolic execution, distributional generation, and situated reference coexist. This hybridity qualifies but does not cancel the indexical turn at the level of interaction and educational practice. Fourth, we articulate three transformations: from “object to think with” to “agent to think with”; from rule-first instruction to abductively initiated inquiry coordinating abduction, induction, and deduction; and from bricolage to artistic navigation. Navigational thinking has logical priority while the relevant problem space remains unstabilized, although it interleaves recursively with computational thinking as inquiry develops. The paper is conceptual rather than empirical: it advances a theoretical account intended to orient subsequent developmental research and pedagogical realization.

items.title: The Role of Inclusive HR Practice in Neurodiverse Talent Retention in International Business Environment: A Qualitative Inquiry
items.abstract: Neurodiversity inclusion is increasingly relevant to international business, yet limited evidence explains how inclusive HR practices shape neurodivergent talent retention and career development. This study explores HR practices and perceptions of inclusiveness in international business contexts. A semi-structured interview method was used in a qualitative interpretivist design consisting of 12 participants, five HR professionals, three supervisors, and four neurodivergent employees. The analysis was done mainly with inductive reflexive thematic analysis with the help of ATLAS.ti software. The six themes that emerged were symbolic inclusion, the lack of formal human resource policies, the implementation by the managers, the strain of the workplace and the psychological strain, the impact on job satisfaction, career progression and retention, and the need for structured training and policy-based changes. The results identify gaps between intended HR practices and employees’ experiences. In conclusion, this study highlights the significance of having consistent policies, managerial skills, flexible adjustments, and structured support to ensure the retention of talent with the brain wiring of ADHD and autism internationally. items.title: The Serendiptionnaire: a Questionnaire for Measuring Experienced Serendipity
items.abstract: Serendipity is important to design for, yet it remains difficult to measure and evaluate. No validated questionnaire exists, so studies either borrow ResQue's novelty scale, which does not measure serendipity, or build their own items, which makes findings hard to compare and synthesize. Building on our earlier conceptualization of experienced serendipity as a fortuitous encounter with content that is both refreshing and enriching, we developed the Serendiptionnaire, a questionnaire that operationalizes our framework. We conducted twenty-seven cognitive interviews over three iterations with respondents who varied in age, education level, country of birth, and English proficiency, while they browsed recommendations on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Spotify. After each iteration, we revised the items until respondents interpreted them as intended. The resulting instrument consists of modular scales that researchers can combine to target the specific flavor of serendipity they want to study or design for. The Serendiptionnaire offers a ground truth for validating system-centered serendipity metrics and LLM-based evaluations, and it provides a nuanced evaluation of users' experienced serendipity.

items.title: The Small-Encoder Crossover Is a Prompted-Baseline Artefact: A Fine-Tuned Encoder Head Loses to a Fine-Tuned 4B Decision Model by 0.33 and to a Majority-Class Control
items.abstract: Every public “a small encoder wins” result we were able to locate inside the target corpus compares that encoder against a prompted (zero- or few-shot) LLM, never against a fine-tuned generative decider (the claim and its audit trail are internal to the corpus, not an external survey — §2). That a fine-tuned generative decider can beat a fine-tuned encoder at comparable effort is already public— a 2025 practitioner blog post reports exactly that on a binary ADE task (§2.1) — so we claim no priority for the direction; what we claim is this fixture, its controls and its diagnosis. We measure the fine-tuned comparison on a sealed typed-single-label decision fixture. Headline. The best fine-tuned encoder head scores 0.3474 and loses to the fine-tuned 4B decider at 0.6789 — the declared primary baseline (author decision 2026-10-15), the auditable same-run arm — with paired McNemar b = 27, c = 90, ψ = 0.616, ∆ = −0.3316, exact p = 4.167e−09. The control that could have contradicted this is the mandatory majority-class control, and it did contradict the candidate’s framing of itself: majority-class returns 0.4526, beating every fine-tuned encoder head by +0.1053. The second control that could have contradicted the measurement is the shuffled-label arm, and it moved the other way from a spurious win: it returns 0.2316, below the fixture’s 0.2911 chance floor. A third control guards instrument integrity: our n-gram leak criterion (≥ 2 distinct shared 8-grams within one row pair, both directions) flagged 0 of 152,000 training↔fixture pairs — and, to show the criterion can fire, it flagged three deliberately seeded copies at 13 / 44 / 57 shared 8-grams (pair maxima). Against the published, pre-registered baseline 0.6684 — which cannot be re-scored from the tree — the same head loses by 0.3210 (“0.32”) against the secondary baseline 0.6684. The two figures use two baselines and must not be read as one: the headline 0.3316 (“0.33”) is computed against the declared primary 0.6789, while 0.3210 (“0.32”) is computed against the secondary/published 0.6684, which is the pre-registered F1 threshold and which cannot be re-scored from the tree. Correction carried. Fixing three defects lowered the SetFit-MPNet arm monotonically (0.3158 → 0.2947 → 0.2632), but the same order-probe fix raised the ModernBERT-base arm (0.342105 → 0.347368). The universal claim “every correction moved the affected arm down” is false; the SetFit arm returned the opposite direction from the ModernBERT arm, which is the control on that claim. Not in this paper. We make no latency claim: the encoder heads were timed locally in one forward batch while the 4B figures come from a served stack’s stored rows, so the tree cannot support a fair latency comparison (see §6.1). We also do not report κ = 0.9014 (first blind reader) or κ = 0.8577 (second, independent blind reader) — nor their mutual κ = 0.9125 —as inter-annotator agreement: both labellers were models, so this is machine reproducibility of the fixture, not human agreement. The second reader partially replicates the first: the κ magnitude holds (both ≥ 0.85) but the exact 0.90 headline does not. An independent human labeller is still owed (§6.2).

items.title: The use of artificial intelligence in patent ductus arteriosus diagnosis and treatment: a systematic scoping review
items.abstract: Background. Background and objectives: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a common congenital cardiac condition, especially in premature infants, and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to aid clinicians in diagnosing PDA and guiding treatment decisions amidst this uncertainty. Methods. A literature search (up to December 2025) was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies on AI (including machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and predictive analytics) applied to PDA. Results. Seventeen studies were included, predominantly involving preterm neonates. AI applications mainly targeted PDA diagnosis and outcome prediction using clinical and echocardiographic data. Imaging-based deep learning models generally outperformed tabular data approaches (with area under the curve often >0.80). Overall study quality was moderate, with limited external validation and data transparency. Conclusions. AI has the potential to transform patent ductus arteriosus management by enabling earlier detection, more consistent decision-making, and individualized treatment planning. Integration of AI into PDA care may reduce practice variability, improve clinical outcomes, and serve as a model for the broader application of artificial intelligence in medicine.

items.title: The Validity of AI-Generated Multiple-Choice Questions for Students With Disabilities
items.abstract: Classroom assessments must meet the rigorous validity standards required for students with disabilities. This study evaluates whether artificial intelligence (AI) can be a reliable partner in the high-stakes environment of special education data collection by examining the validity of multiple-choice questions generated by three large-language-model chatbots (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini). Each chatbot produced 200 items under default and deeper settings (N = 600) and items were scored against 15 objective item-writing guidelines. Models frequently violated rules about complete stems and randomized key placement, with ChatGPT having the highest overall error rate and Copilot and Gemini the lowest. Chi-square and ANOVA analyses showed significant differences across chatbots, especially for specific guidelines, while deeper prompts improved quality only slightly. Results suggest AI can rapidly draft items with solid, plausible distractors, but educators must review and revise them to ensure their quality.

items.abstract: Abstract This chapter proposes a novel integrative framework for AI-driven marketing innovation ecosystems (MIEs) that links service-dominant logic, ecosystem-as-structure theory, platform governance, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled value co-creation. By uniting these theoretical perspectives, the proposed framework addresses critical conceptual aspects in ecosystems and new technology-related marketing theory. It provides a marketing-specific ecosystem model, clarifies how to align diverse actors around shared value propositions in AI-intensive contexts, and examines novel governance challenges (such as ensuring algorithmic transparency and managing power asymmetries among ecosystem participants) posed by AI technologies. This conceptual chapter explores how AI reshapes ecosystem roles, interactions, and co-creation dynamics by blurring traditional producer–consumer boundaries, facilitating new forms of collaborative innovation across stakeholders, and necessitating adaptive governance mechanisms. This chapter clarifies how AI reshapes structural alignment, actor roles, and value co-creation dynamics within MIEs, emphasizing that AI demands adaptive governance mechanisms to address algorithmic transparency, ethical considerations, and power asymmetries.

items.title: Toward AI-Ready Paper-Based Colorimetric Glucose Sensing: Selectivity, Sensitivity, and Standardized High-Throughput Data Generation
items.abstract: Paper-based colorimetric glucose sensing has evolved from simple visual assays toward digitally quantified systems increasingly supported by artificial intelligence (AI). However, advanced computational analysis cannot fully compensate for limitations in sensing hardware or for insufficient and poorly standardized analytical data. In this Perspective, we argue that truly AI-ready paper-based glucose sensing requires coordinated development of three capabilities: selective molecular input, sensitive and reproducible signal generation, and standardized high-throughput data generation. Selective input can be engineered through filtering and permselective interfaces; signal generation can be strengthened through catalytic amplification, enzyme stabilization, reagent organization, and reaction-microenvironment engineering; and standardized paper platforms can provide the large, comparable datasets required for robust machine-learning models. We discuss these developments in the context of paper-based glucose assays and propose an integrated framework in which sensing chemistry, device architecture, dataset design, and computational analysis are co-designed. Such integration shifts AI from compensating for limitations of individual assays toward extracting robust quantitative information from intrinsically selective, informative, and reproducible analytical data.

items.title: Toward Effective Remote Operation in Automated Rail Transport: Insights From an Expert Evaluation
items.abstract: This study investigates the design of an effective remote operator workplace for supervising automated train systems. As railway automation advances, remote operation is expected to play a critical role as a fallback solution, particularly in situations requiring human intervention. While previous research has focused on remote control during system disruptions, limited attention has been given to standard operations such as shunting. To address this gap, a human-centered design approach was applied, including expert workshops and iterative prototyping. Five experts in human factors and automation participated in a structured workshop to define requirements and design a prototypical human-machine interface. The results highlight the importance of task allocation between automation and human operators. The prototype includes four monitors, dual touchpads for interaction and communication, and additional control elements such as an emergency stop button and auditory feedback systems. Overall, the study highlights the importance of human centered design for effective automated railway systems.

items.title: Toward temporal stability in explainable AI: A framework for measuring explanation drift
items.abstract: Adaptive recommender systems are updated as new user interactions occur. These updates can change both the recommendations and explanations produced by the system. However, most explainable artificial intelligence methods evaluate explanations at a single point in time and do not measure how they change during continual updates. This study investigates explanation drift in dynamic graph-based recommender systems. We propose a temporal framework that combines graph representation learning, streaming embedding updates, Shapley-based feature attribution, and drift-aware optimization. The framework uses three measures: Temporal Attribution Divergence (TAD), Explanation Stability Score (ESS), and Explanation Half-Life (EHL). We evaluated the approach on MovieLens-1M and an Amazon Product Reviews subset under continual update settings. The proposed framework achieved an F1@10 of 0.837 on MovieLens-1M, compared with 0.821 for the strongest reported baseline, and 0.810 on Amazon, compared with 0.789. It also reduced the TAD by approximately 42.2% compared with the Static SHAP and increased the ESS from 0.612 to 0.831. These results show that explanation changes can be reduced while maintaining the recommendation performance in the tested settings. The evaluation is limited to offline benchmark datasets and feature-attribution stability and does not measure how users understand or judge the explanations. These results support the use of temporal explanation stability as an additional evaluation measure for adaptive recommender systems.

items.title: Toward unified intelligence in renewable-dominant power systems: a survey of hybrid forecasting, explainable AI, and multi-agent optimization
items.abstract: The transition toward renewable-dominant power systems has introduced significant operational challenges due to increased uncertainty, reduced system inertia, and the proliferation of distributed energy resources. While artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have been widely adopted for renewable energy forecasting and grid optimization, existing studies primarily address these components in isolation, leading to fragmented system-level intelligence. This paper presents a comprehensive survey that systematically integrates three critical dimensions of modern intelligent energy systems: hybrid forecasting, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multi-agent optimization. First, we review advanced hybrid learning architectures, including decomposition-based models, ensemble frameworks, and deep learning-metaheuristic hybrids, highlighting their effectiveness in capturing nonlinear and stochastic renewable dynamics. Second, we examine XAI techniques that enhance transparency, interpretability, and trust in AI-driven energy systems. Third, we analyze the evolution from centralized optimization to distributed collective intelligence using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), swarm intelligence, and federated learning paradigms. Unlike conventional surveys, this work provides a unified system-level perspective by explicitly linking predictive uncertainty with decentralized decision-making and explainability mechanisms. A conceptual integration framework is presented to demonstrate how probabilistic forecasting, risk-aware MARL policies, and interpretable models can jointly enable robust and scalable grid operation. Furthermore, we identify key research challenges related to scalability, computational efficiency, uncertainty propagation, and real-time deployment. This survey offers a structured reference for researchers and practitioners and outlines future directions toward trustworthy, adaptive, and cooperative AI-driven energy systems.

items.title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
items.abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.

items.title: Traditional AI, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Executive AI: A Comprehensive Comparative Review
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) can encompass a system's ability to make predictions, create content, plan, use tools, and inform decisions. Furthermore, these capabilities tend to overlap, and the basic approach of treating each of these as four discrete steps risks creating a false impression. Specifically, this review explores Traditional AI, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Executive AI through a common framework of questions regarding goals, objectives, autonomy, planning, action, resources, memory, learning, governance, and metrics of success. In this context, Traditional AI is treated as a broad category of techniques that accomplish tasks such as prediction, classification, search, and improvement. Similarly, Generative AI is considered a broad category of techniques that produce content. Additionally, Agentic AI is defined as a set of systems that are arranged to execute steps toward solving specified tasks. Conversely, Executive AI is introduced as a proposed goal-directed coordination architecture that aims to bridge a long-term goal to smaller tasks, their potential pathways, personnel, tools, resources, feedback, and metrics of outcome achievement. Methodologically, this is a concept-driven narrative review of selected work on topics such as foundational research, surveys, planning, and official guidance. Ultimately, the proposed comparison provides an improved vocabulary for discussing AI systems and outlines the empirical experiments required to assess whether goal-level coordination is advantageous.

items.title: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
items.abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.

items.title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
items.abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.

items.title: TRAM-AI: A Framework for Transparency in Reporting of Medical Imaging Datasets for Artificial Intelligence Development
items.abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate TRAM-AI, a consensus-based checklist for verifying whether medical imaging datasets described as publicly accessible are functionally usable for AI development. Materials and Methods A modified Delphi study was conducted. A steering committee generated candidate checklist items through a targeted literature review. An international expert panel ( n = 33) rated items on criticality and feasibility across two Delphi rounds. Consensus was defined as ≥ 75% agreement on both dimensions. The checklist was pilot-validated in 10 publicly available datasets. An advisory group of four experts from Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa evaluated cross-regional applicability. Results Of 16 candidate items, 14 were retained in the final checklist; one item was removed because of feasibility concerns, and another was merged with an existing item because of conceptual redundancy. All 14 final items achieved consensus for both criticality and feasibility. The final TRAM-AI checklist comprises 14 items across four domains: Dataset Access and Persistence (3 items), Technical Interoperability (4 items), Metadata and Reproducibility (4 items), and Ethical, Legal, and Maintenance considerations (3 items). In pilot validation, all items were applicable to all 10 datasets, compliance was 90% for trusted repository, de-dentification, and subject-level mapping, 10% for archive validation, and 30% for partition keys. All four advisory group members endorsed the checklist. Conclusion TRAM-AI provides a practical framework for verifying the functional accessibility of medical imaging datasets, complementing existing methodological reporting standards. Further evaluation and broader validation across diverse geographic settings are warranted. ©RSNA, 2026

items.title: Transforming the business model innovation process: how generative artificial intelligence shapes value creation, delivery, and capture
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) may transform the Business Model Innovation (BMI) process and under which conditions it may reshape core Business Model (BM) mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review of 131 peer-reviewed articles was conducted. Using the Gioia methodology in an abductive analysis, with the 4I-framework of BMI as a sensitizing lens, an integrative framework was developed to synthesize GenAI's role across BMI phases and BM mechanisms. Findings The findings show that GenAI supports all phases of the BMI process by enhancing opportunity recognition, ideation, experimentation, and implementation through the mechanisms of knowledge amplification, cognitive catalysis, and methodological scaffolding. Beyond process support, GenAI can reshape value creation through hyper-personalized and content-centric offerings, alter value delivery through hybrid human-AI service architectures, and extend value capture through efficiency gains and data-driven revenue logics. Whether such effects remain operational augmentation or amount to BM adaptation and transformation depends on their embedding in the BM architecture. At the same time, these effects remain conditioned by data governance, model opacity, ethical and regulatory risk, and workforce capabilities, suggesting GenAI's role in BMI is ambivalent: it may enable innovation while also creating new constraints for its realization. Research limitations/implications The review is conceptual and cross-sectoral. Future research should empirically test the proposed mechanisms and examine industry- and context-specific boundary conditions. Practical implications Firms should treat GenAI as a strategic lever for BMI and complement adoption with robust governance, human oversight, and workforce capability development. Originality/value The study offers a process-oriented synthesis of GenAI-enabled BMI and develops an integrative framework linking BMI phases, GenAI-enabled process mechanisms, and BM mechanisms while identifying key boundary conditions shaping GenAI-enabled BMI.

items.title: Transitioning from traditional hospital design to activity-based care: A longitudinal case study of differential occupational health and safety consequences across clinical settings and professional roles
items.abstract: The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation.

items.title: Trends in soil organic carbon prediction research using geospatial technologies and artificial intelligence: an exploratory bibliometric analysis (2005-2025)
items.abstract: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is central to soil fertility and climate regulation, and its spatial prediction increasingly relies on geospatial technologies and artificial intelligence (AI). Existing bibliometric studies and reviews have examined remote sensing-based soil organic matter monitoring, agricultural SOC components, or digital soil mapping separately, a bibliometric synthesis of how these strands have converged into GeoAI (geospatial AI: the integration of AI with spatially explicit data) for SOC prediction is lacking. This study presents an exploratory bibliometric analysis of SOC prediction research from 2005 to 2025. Scopus was searched on 25 March 2026 with a field-tagged Boolean query restricted to English-language journal articles, after screening and duplicate removal, 1561 articles were analyzed with Bibliometrix in R (performance analysis, co-authorship, co-citation, keyword co-occurrence). The annual growth rate was 28.68%, output rose sharply after 2018 and exceeded 300 articles in 2024, 40.49% of articles involved international co-authorship, and documents averaged 43.67 citations. China and the United States led in total citations (16,602 and 8,006, respectively), and China led in output. Geoderma, Science of the Total Environment, and Environmental Monitoring and Assessment were the most frequent sources, keyword analysis identified machine learning, remote sensing, and digital soil mapping as the methodological core. Output, citations and collaboration were concentrated in a few countries, with Africa, South Asia, and parts of Latin America underrepresented, which may limit model transferability, causes were not measured. items.title: TrustedCode: Evaluating Large Language Models for Developing Trusted Code through Automated Program Verification
items.abstract: Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30\% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI-generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI-generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type-check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back-end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain-of-thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50\% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30\% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20\% from semantic and type-related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM-guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \href{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}. The video demonstration is available at: \href{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}

items.title: Two for One: Privileged Learning for Resource-Constrained Screening
items.abstract: Machine learning systems are often developed under data-rich conditions but deployed when only incomplete information is available. A natural example arises in colour fundus photography (CFP), where both eyes are commonly imaged because they can provide complementary information for ocular disease assessment. Prior approaches that exploit bilateral information either fuse both eyes in a single model or use knowledge distillation to compress a dual-eye teacher into a lightweight student that still requires both images at test time. However, bilateral acquisition may not always be feasible. We thus propose a privileged learning framework in which a teacher model has access to bilateral CFP images during training and learns representations informed by information from both eyes, while the student is trained to transfer this knowledge from the bilateral teacher using only a single-eye image as input. At inference, the student operates exclusively on this single-eye input and does not require the contralateral image. Experimental results show consistent improvements in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve over conventional monocular training, with the largest gains observed for left-eye images for the detection of age-related macular degeneration (0.931 vs. 0.966) and diabetic retinopathy (0.789 vs. 0.836).%, while requiring only a single-eye image at inference. By enabling models to benefit from bilateral information during training while requiring only a single-eye image at inference, our approach may support more reliable deployment in resource-constrained clinical and screening environments.

items.abstract: Crop-disease triage from field imagery is routinely evaluated as if each pixel carried a single ground-truth label, yet phytopathologists disagree systematically about lesion boundaries, and that disagreement is not noise to be averaged away but evidence about which regions are genuinely ambiguous. The framework is characterised analytically rather than empirically: no observational data are used or claimed. A before-after-control-impact design is specified under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), and the operating characteristics of the design are derived across 2000 replications per cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point improvement at 80% power under this variance structure, and it formalises the conditions under which deferral improves expected triage utility relative to forced labelling. The contribution is a decision-theoretic account of when an evidential segmenter should be trusted, deferred or overruled in agricultural triage, together with the design parameters that make such an evaluation identifiable.

items.title: Understanding Users' Stickiness in AI-Enabled Cloud Services From the Perspective of Process Virtualization Theory and Switching Costs
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cloud services are increasingly embedded in users' daily activities, yet little is known about how user stickiness develops in virtualized service environments. Drawing on process virtualization theory, uses and gratifications theory, and switching costs, this study examines how process virtualization capability shapes user stickiness through sociability gratification and usage gratification. Survey data from 443 AI cloud service users were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that process virtualization capability positively affects both forms of gratification, which increase user stickiness. Switching costs weaken the effect of sociability gratification on stickiness but do not significantly moderate the effect of usage gratification. The study extends research on AI cloud services by distinguishing social and functional gratification pathways to user stickiness and showing how their sensitivity to switching costs differs.

items.title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
items.abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

items.title: Unlocking Spatial Grounding in Flow-Matching Models via SNR Tuning
items.abstract: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.

items.title: Validating Autoformalized Specifications via Contrapuntal Languages
items.abstract: Formal specifications can make AI-generated code mechanically checkable. Because user intent is typically expressed in natural language rather than formal logic, specifications must first be derived from it, e.g., via LLM-based autoformalization. Yet autoformalized specifications are themselves untrusted, so a key challenge is validating whether they capture user intent without relying on a costly oracle such as human review. In this oracle-free setting, a natural strategy is to vote among model outputs, but because model errors are often correlated, agreement among outputs may reflect shared mistakes rather than correctness. Our key insight is that these errors can be decorrelated through representational diversity. We achieve this diversity with contrapuntal languages: pairs of task-specific formal languages, each designed to express the intended specification, yet admitting no structure-preserving translation between them. An LLM formalizes the intent independently in each language, and we accept a specification only if a solver proves the two formalizations equivalent. To construct such languages, we present a synthesis algorithm that reuses fragments of sampled seed specifications as syntactic sugar over a base specification language. We implement the approach for first-order logic specifications and evaluate it on HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench using GPT-5.4 mini and Qwen3.6-Flash with and without thinking. Over the strongest baseline, our method increases the proportion of accepted specifications that are correct, i.e., complete and sound, by 12.0% on HumanEval+ and 42.9% on LiveCodeBench. The accepted specifications judged complete reject 98.6% of buggy program variants on HumanEval+ and 96.2% on LiveCodeBench, compared with 92.8% and 78.3% for the strongest baseline.

items.title: Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy: A Conceptual Framework for Governing Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Business-to-Business Credit Risk Management
items.abstract: Firms that sell to other firms on credit now face a new design choice. Software agents built on large language models can gather evidence, draft credit memos, release held orders and chase overdue invoices. Yet there is little guidance on how much of this work an agent should do without a person. Most research on artificial intelligence in credit asks how accurate a model is, and most of it studies consumer lending. It says little about the decision rights of autonomous agents in business-to-business trade credit, where much activity sits outside consumer-protection and bank model-risk rules. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. It integrates research on trade credit, credit scoring, language-model agents, levels of automation, agency theory and model-risk governance. From this synthesis it builds the Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy framework. The central claim is simple: the autonomy granted to an agent should rise with the verifiability of the evidence behind a decision and fall with the decision's financial exposure and irreversibility. The paper defines four autonomy tiers and a transparent allocation rule. It maps twelve common trade-credit decisions onto the tiers. It proposes a Propose–Verify–Dispose architecture in which language-model agents propose, deterministic checks verify, and policy rules or people dispose. It offers seven testable propositions and four measures for future empirical work. For managers, the framework turns a vague question, "can we trust the agent?", into a concrete design rule that fits existing delegation-of-authority practice. Keywords: large language model agents; trade credit; delegation of authority; model risk management; human oversight

items.title: VeruSteer: Learning What to Repair Next in Verus
items.abstract: LLM-based verification systems repair Rust proofs by revising programs in response to Verus diagnostics. When several error types are reported, pipelines such as AutoVerus and VeruSAGE select the next repair target using a preset priority. Yet each repair changes the program and the errors that follow, so the same reported types can require different choices at different states. We present VeruSteer, which learns to select error types from the outcomes of alternative repair trajectories. It constructs repair trees offline and compares paths from the same initial program by verification success, repair rounds, and final verification progress. These comparisons supervise a selector that combines step-wise imitation with trajectory preference ranking. The selector uses self-attention over the program, verifier feedback, and earlier selections to rank the currently reported types. It replaces the default priority within a single repair trajectory, keeping the existing repair agents and adding no repair or verifier calls for selection. We evaluate VeruSteer by replaying its choices on stored AutoVerus and VeruSAGE test trees under four generation configurations. Across 1,270 test trees, VeruSteer increases verified outcomes from 185 to 194 (14.57\% to 15.28\%), gaining 12 successes and losing three for a net improvement of 0.71 percentage points. Among trees where the default fails but a recorded alternative verifies, VeruSteer succeeds on 3 of 4 AutoVerus trees and 9 of 11 VeruSAGE trees. Among trees with recorded alternatives where the default verifies, it retains success on 14 of 15 AutoVerus trees and 12 of 14 VeruSAGE trees. It also finds shorter successful trajectories and improves final progress on some trees where all recorded trajectories fail.

The findings also offer practical implications for designing healthier meeting practices, supporting sustainable remote and hybrid work arrangements, and informing organizational policies on digital collaboration.

items.title: Virtual Frontliners: A Study on the Psychosocial Effects and Coping Mechanisms of Filipino Healthcare Virtual Assistants
items.abstract: This study, titled “Virtual Frontliners: A Study on the Psychosocial Effects and Coping Mechanisms of Filipino Healthcare Virtual Assistants,” explored the lived psychosocial experiences and coping mechanisms of Filipino healthcare virtual assistants (HVAs) engaged in remote healthcare-related work. The study examined the demands associated with healthcare support work, the emotional and social effects of working remotely, the strategies participants used to manage stress, and the forms of organizational support they considered helpful. The study employed a qualitative descriptive phenomenological design. Eight Filipino healthcare virtual assistants were purposively selected based on the study criteria. Data were generated through individual semi-structured interviews conducted remotely through Zoom or Google Meet. Prior to the interview, informed consent was completed electronically through Google Forms. The interviews lasted approximately 20–30 minutes and explored participants’ work demands, psychosocial experiences, work-life boundaries, job satisfaction and motivation, coping, workplace resources, and suggested support strategies. With participant consent, the interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed for analysis. The interview transcripts were analyzed using a Colaizzi-guided descriptive phenomenological procedure. The researcher repeatedly read the complete transcripts, extracted significant statements, formulated meanings, clustered related meanings into themes, developed an exhaustive description, and synthesized the fundamental structure of the experience. Five major themes emerged: Accuracy Under Pressure; Flexibility, Boundaries, and Disconnection; Strain, Growth, and Meaning; Structured Coping and Recovery; and Resources and Support Shape Well-Being. The findings showed that the participants experienced remote HVA work as demanding but meaningful, with psychosocial well-being shaped by the balance between job demands and available personal, social, and organizational resources. The participants commonly relied on task prioritization, breaks, rest and sleep, family time, deliberate work-life boundaries, and help-seeking. They identified clear communication, training, reliable work systems, manageable workloads, regular check-ins, peer connection, wellness resources, and recognition as important forms of support. items.title: Virtual Reality Dance Practices: The Pedagogical Potential of Using Immersive Learning Environments for Developing Emotional Intelligence
items.abstract: Developing emotional intelligence (EI) in higher education requires innovative pedagogical approaches supported by objective assessment methods. This study evaluated the effectiveness of an immersive virtual reality (VR) dance intervention for enhancing EI among Chinese university students by integrating motion analysis, physiological measurements, and computational modeling. A randomized controlled trial involving 145 participants was conducted over an eight-week intervention period. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: immersive VR dance training using head-mounted displays, two-dimensional (2D) screen-based dance instruction, or a control group receiving no practical training. Emotional intelligence was assessed using the Mayer–Salovey–Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT) before the intervention, immediately afterward, and at a four-week follow-up. Motion kinematics, physiological indicators, and computational analyses were integrated to evaluate learning outcomes. In addition, an exploratory algorithmic personalization approach adapted the training protocol to individual participant characteristics. Participants in the VR group demonstrated an average improvement of 18.5 MSCEIT points (Cohen’s d = 1.68) together with a 34.2% increase in movement amplitude. Improvements in the 2D group were substantially smaller (7.3 points; d = 0.51), while the control group showed only minimal gains (2.1 points). The exploratory personalization analysis suggested an additional 23% improvement in intervention effectiveness. At the four-week follow-up, participants retained 76.2% of the acquired gains.

items.title: VR Phobia Desensitization with Haptics: Dose-Response Curves for Vibrotactile Cues in Graded Exposure
items.abstract: Virtual reality exposure therapy provides a controlled, adjustable method for phobia desensitization, but treatment effectiveness depends on careful calibration of exposure intensity. This study evaluated vibrotactile haptics as a graded design variable in VR phobia treatment, emphasizing dose-response effects across exposure stages. Participants completed repeated VR exposure sessions under four haptic conditions: minimal or no haptics, low-dose feedback, moderate-dose feedback, and high-dose vibrotactile cues. Feedback varied in amplitude, duration, and timing, including event-linked and sustained vibration patterns. Outcomes included fear activation, habituation, progression, early termination, perceived control, presence, workload, and acceptability. Results showed a non-linear dose-response relationship. Moderate feedback produced the strongest therapeutic and usability profile by increasing engagement and fear activation while remaining tolerable enough to support progression and habituation. Higher doses increased realism and arousal but also caused distraction, overload, and greater early-termination risk. Carefully calibrated haptics may therefore strengthen VR phobia treatment across diverse users and stages.

items.title: Water management in flood-prone areas using nature-based solutions: an AI-assisted systematic review and thematic analysis
items.abstract: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly used to reduce flood risk and improve water management in flood-prone areas. However, research remains fragmented across disciplines, regions, and scales, making it difficult to identify research trends, knowledge gaps, and priorities. This study presents an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted systematic review of peer-reviewed articles published between 2016 and 2025, retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, a large language model (LLM) was used to screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review by the research team. A structured dataset was developed through LLM-assisted data extraction and human validation. Semantic clustering and LLM-assisted synthesis were then used to identify research themes and summarize implementation conditions, benefits, limitations, and research needs. A total of 185 studies were included, which were predominantly published between 2021 and 2025. Nine research themes emerged, with urban green infrastructure for runoff mitigation, spatial planning and decision support, and catchment and hydraulic modeling accounting for 47.6% of the studies. Research was concentrated in the United Kingdom, China, and the United States, with limited representation from Africa and Latin America. The evidence relied mainly on scenario modeling and short monitoring periods, while social equity, public acceptance, and maintenance outcomes were rarely assessed using standardized metrics. While literature reviews have been previously done on the topic of NbS for flood-prone water management, to our knowledge, this is the first review of NbS for flood-prone water management to combine LLM-assisted screening, data extraction, and synthesis with semantic clustering and human validation. The study provides a thematic evidence map, examines temporal and geographic research trends, and presents a reproducible workflow to support future environmental evidence synthesis.

items.title: Wearables in the Drop Zone: Human-Centered Design of a Sensor Sock for Airborne Training
items.abstract: Military airborne training exposes soldiers to high biomechanical loads during parachute landing falls (PLFs), contributing to persistent lower-extremity injury risk. While ankle braces exist that reduce injury, operational adoption is very low. This paper presents a human-centered design case study focused on the development of a wearable sensor sock for assessing PLF biomechanics and supporting training evaluation. Stakeholder engagement, operational site visits, and laboratory testing were used to iteratively refine the wearable system’s sensing strategy, wearability, and integration within existing training workflows. The prototype integrated force sensing resistors, inertial measurement units, strain sensors, and electromyography sensors to measure plantar loading, landing impact characteristics, ankle kinematics, and lower-leg muscle activation patterns relevant to PLF performance. Key lessons learned highlight the importance of designing wearable systems that align with user culture, instructional practice, and the realities of field deployment.

items.title: What the Trace Shows and What the Label Says: Auditing Behavioral Detectors in Agent Evaluation
items.abstract: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, and they may not fully capture what the trace shows. We study this in a tool-use setting built on GSM8K, where agents call a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, giving clear ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported. We audit three trace-level detectors across six production models and 30 problems per model. Final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation can disagree in systematic ways. A key failure mode is silent tool-output override: the calculator returns a corrupted value, but the model later uses a different, often correct, value without calling the tool again, so the bad value stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review of 90 traces agrees perfectly with the automated labels for final correctness (67/67), fault impact (19/19), and fault relevance (18/18), but only 67/81 for verification; all 14 disagreements fall into four recurring patterns. Execution limits also change the reported result: in an ablation across two models, one ranges from 21/30 to 27/30 correct as step and token budgets change, while the other stays between 27/30 and 29/30. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should come with the trace evidence behind it, whether the question the detector asks applied to that trace, whether the run was cut off by an execution limit, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.

items.title: When AI advice agrees or disagrees with human judgment: trust, self-efficacy, psychological resilience, and adaptive responses in physical education
items.abstract: As AI-based decision-support systems become increasingly embedded in physical education and coaching practice, agreement and disagreement between algorithmic advice and participants’ immediate scenario judgments have become important but theoretically underexamined features of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in a shared Judge-Advisor System paradigm, four scenario-based experiments (total N = 859) manipulated whether an experimentally presented AI recommendation was consistent or conflicting with each participant’s prior judgment and tested machine trust and collaborative decision-making self-efficacy as psychological pathways to self-reported collaborative adaptive responses. Psychological resilience and rationale provision were examined as study-specific boundary conditions. Conflict significantly reduced machine trust (Study 1, d = 1.061) and self-efficacy (Study 2, B = −0.687), and both measured mediators carried significant negative indirect associations with adaptive responses (Study 1, B = −0.428; Study 2, via trust B = −0.201, via self-efficacy B = −0.127). Psychological resilience attenuated the between-condition difference in self-efficacy in Study 3 (index of moderated mediation = 0.115). In Study 4, rationale provision moderated the condition-to-trust association, F (1, 239) = 11.348, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.045: the conflict effect was −0.811 in the black-box condition but −0.182 when a rationale was provided. The manipulation therefore concerns advice-judgment agreement rather than a direct experimental comparison of data-driven judgment with established experiential intuition. Because the scenarios did not establish objective recommendation accuracy, the moderation patterns are interpreted as changes in psychological response rather than as evidence that preserving trust or self-efficacy necessarily improves calibration, decision quality, or welfare.

items.title: When AI Enters the Pencil Box: A Longitudinal Study of Child–LLM Writing Collaboration in a Chinese Primary School
items.abstract: We report a qualitative study spanning more than six months with upper-primary students (ages 9–12) in southern China using a local LLM (Doubao) for writing. Two interview waves with ten students (nine re-interviewed) and six teachers (three re-interviewed) reveal a set of recurring shifts in our focal cohort: from novelty to strategy, from anthropomorphic “companion/virtual teacher” to tool-like framing, and from quick unsticking to guarded use shaped by dependence, fairness, and exam-transfer Footnote1 concerns. Students valued speed and breadth but noted mechanical tone, age/style mismatch, and weak transfer to AI-free tests. We map a Control × Dependency framework and before/after transitions, and surface tensions around classroom norms and equity amid policy ambiguity and uneven AI literacy. We suggest process-visible, agency-preserving integration: sentence- and phrase-level provenance with mandatory micro-edits, task-specific scaffold ceilingsFootnote2, and process-anchored assessment schemes that explicitly factor in AI-use traces.

items.title: When does AI dependence for decisions trigger moral disengagement? A proposed model with ethical position as a moderator
items.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to present a conceptual model investigating the moderating role of individuals’ ethical positions (idealism and relativism) in the relationship between dependence on artificial intelligence (AI) for decisions and moral disengagement. Design/methodology/approach Theoretical explanations and logical connections among the variables are developed within a propositional framework by integrating conservation of resources theory, social cognitive theory and ethics position theory, informed by research on algorithmic decision-making and moral disengagement. Findings This study proposes that dependence on AI for decisions is positively associated with moral disengagement. Idealism is expected to weaken this relationship, whereas relativism is expected to strengthen it where organisational performance demands favour accepting AI recommendations despite foreseeable stakeholder harm. The model concerns employees who retain meaningful discretion over AI-supported decisions. Practical implications Organisations should provide meaningful opportunities to question and escalate AI recommendations and examine whether performance expectations discourage ethical review. Training should address stakeholder harm and responsibility-displacing rationalisations. Originality/value This study distinguishes dependence on AI for decisions from general AI usage and restrictions on employee autonomy. It develops an explanation of how such dependence may facilitate moral disengagement and identifies idealism and relativism as distinct boundary conditions, specifying the context of the proposed strengthening effect of relativism.
